title: Trump vs. America
excerpt: If Donald Trump has maintained one pretense continuously throughout his career in politics, it is that his entire goal is to help the United States of America
body: If Donald Trump has maintained one pretense continuously throughout his career in politics, it is that his entire goal is to help the United States of America
The founding conceit of the first Trump campaign was that he would set aside his business interests, at great personal expense, to rescue the country he loved
It was embedded in his slogans (“America First,” “Make America Great Again”) and his palace-building binge, which he naturally justified as his service to the symbols of the country
Finally, at a press conference this afternoon, he broke character
The CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins asked the president a question about his comment earlier this week to Vladimir Putin

Seeing the Russian dictator, Trump broke into a wide smile, perhaps a more genuine expression of delight than he has ever displayed before in public, and called Putin “my friend.” Collins asked Trump, “You said Putin is your friend
Russia, of course, is Iran’s biggest ally
Do you believe Putin is a friend to America?” Trump replied: “I can’t speak to America
I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, and to be honest, he was very nice about it
It was a hoax that was made up by the Democrats
It probably helped me win the election—re-win the election.” Even by Trumpian standards, this was an extraordinary confession
First, he said he cannot speak for what is good for America, as if the United States were some foreign entity with interests totally inscrutable to him
He then explained that Putin is very good to him personally

Any other world leader caught using covert measures to help a pro-Russian candidate win the American presidency would apparently have been cross, but Putin was “very nice about it,” which just shows what a swell guy he is. [ Philips Payson O’Brien: Trump’s axis of ignorance ] Recall that the Trumpian line has always been that Trump sides with Russia so frequently because he is coldly looking out for the American wallet
Last year, Trump batted away a reporter’s question about his tilt toward Russia by saying, “I’m not aligned with Putin
I’m aligned with the United States of America and for the good of the world.” This week, after Trump’s display of warmth and love toward Putin, J

Vance posted a clip of the encounter and commented on X, “The president will talk to anyone, anywhere, to advocate for American interests.” It was obvious enough, given that Trump had called in to a meeting of Europeans who were supporting Ukraine to urge them to stop doing so

Trump “told Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday they could save money as well as lives by ending the war with Russia, according to five European officials who were briefed on the discussion,” Politico reported
Trump has always claimed to oppose sending aid to Ukraine because he resents sending American money overseas

But his effort to persuade Europeans to stop aiding Ukraine suggests that his actual motivation is that he wants Russia to win because he admires and sympathizes with its leader, his personal friend. “America First” has always meant Trump first.

title: Silicon Valley Is Scrambling Now
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
In The Lord of the Rings , a palantir is a crystal ball that allows users to peer into the future—but it gives only partial information
This might have been a warning to Alex Karp, the CEO of the tech company named Palantir

Earlier this year, Karp crowed that AI would reduce the power of “highly educated, often female voters, who vote mostly Democrat.” Postelection, he’s singing a different tune. “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life

I grew up in a far-left environment,” Karp recently told Politico . “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” He used that last word, progressive , eight times in the interview
Karp also claimed that he’d been critical of Donald Trump in private, though he somehow decided to disclose it only now

His fellow tech titan Elon Musk—once described as Trump’s “co-president” and the biggest donor to his 2024 campaign— now says he’s “not MAGA” and “doesn’t know what MAGA means.” Perhaps he should have inquired before he made MAGA hats part of his wardrobe
Musk’s SpaceX is backing off from referring to the “Gulf of America” too
These flips are particularly brazen (and unconvincing), but they are not unique

On Election Night, as the size of Democrats’ victory became clear, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who had praised the Trump administration for producing a “breath of fresh air” in Silicon Valley, declared , “People should always be in control of the future.” Kalshi abruptly cut ties with Donald Trump Jr

Meanwhile, Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship impresario who’d spoken at the Republican National Convention and whom Trump had recently suggested as White House press secretary, said that he wants “nothing to do with politics.” If he grasped the irony of saying this on Lara Trump’s Fox News show, he didn’t let it on

Jeff Bezos is also tempering his enthusiasm for Trump, saying that he is “on the side of America,” not either party, and noting that he has worked with “every president since Clinton.” VIPs who rushed to get tickets to a Trump crypto gala in years past are no longer so eager

The podcaster Joe Rogan, a major influence on young men who swung to Trump in the 2024 election, is now disillusioned. “They didn’t just lose the podcast bros,” he said. “They lost most of the country.” Emily Litella —the Saturday Night Live character with the catchphrase “Never mind”—would feel right at home with this bunch
The clumsy reversals have inevitably been labeled , in the au courant fashion, a “ vibe shift .” This is perhaps an apt description
Postelection, it is tempting to treat these statements from corporate leaders as evidence of a major paradigm change
In reality, they are better understood as ephemeral marketing

For many years, big companies tried to avoid getting sucked into divisive political issues. (The billionaire Michael Jordan crisply encapsulated the reason when he said, “Republicans buy sneakers too.”) But the killing of George Floyd in 2020, and the enormous demonstrations that followed, led some business leaders to adopt public social-justice stances
Others announced after the January 6 riot that they would no longer donate to election deniers
This drew the ire of Republicans who labeled it “ woke capital ,” a possible contradiction in terms
As I wrote at the time , though, “These corporations are acting in a majoritarian manner

But no one should conclude that they are progressive.” Indeed, when Trump returned to office, the corporate establishment quickly adapted itself to the new regime, moving to accommodate Trump by giving large donations or by shutting down DEI programs. (Some of the companies that had pledged to halt giving to deniers quietly dropped their commitment.) Institutions that forcefully jumped on the Trump bandwagon were responding to analysis that suggested that the 2024 election represented a serious and lasting change in American politics
As it turned out, the shift was just vibes —fleeting and easily dispelled rather than solid and real
By late this summer, the problems of betting on Trump were becoming apparent , and the scale of Democrats’ victories in the midterms now has executives rushing to get back in their good graces
One element of these reversals is that people have shortsighted perspectives on politics, tending to overrate the importance of whatever the most recent election result was
In this century alone, pundits and operatives have declared both major political parties dead, yet they both remain peskily alive
No one should be surprised if executives are just as prone to overestimating the durability of any new ruling coalition

The more important factor, though, is prudent (or, depending on whom you ask, cynical) business concerns: Companies like Palantir and SpaceX rely heavily on government contracts; Kalshi and OpenAI need a friendly regulatory environment
Should a Republican win the 2028 election, expect progressive to vanish from Alex Karp’s vernacular just as quickly as it entered
Big companies will always seek to curry favor, and elected officials are too often susceptible to their flattery, no matter how shallow
These transactional relationships serve both sides well, but they don’t necessarily serve the people

title: What’s So Important About Nvidia’s Chips?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Beyond the salacious details of the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal is a story about national security and the ad
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Beyond the salacious details of the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal is a story about national security and the advanced chips powering the AI boom

But what exactly are these chips, and why do they matter? Ben Buchanan was one of President Biden’s AI advisers and helped write some of the U.S. policies on chip controls, in conversation with people like Huang
In this episode of Galaxy Brain , he breaks down what makes those chips so valuable and why they have such implications for the U.S.-Chinese relationship and the future of AI
The following is a transcript of the episode: Ben Buchanan: We had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia
They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that

But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. [ Music ] Charlie Warzel: The further we get out from the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal, the more it seems clear that, despite all the salacious details, there’s a lot more to this story than meets the eye
It’s an alleged Chinese-spy sex scandal, yes
It’s this huge, Silicon Valley palace-intrigue story
But as time goes by, it seems that the epicenter of this story is in Washington, D.C
The Nvidia–Jensen Huang affair is, at heart, a geopolitical thriller
It is a series of cascading events that’s been set in motion by a cold war between China and the United States over advanced AI chips and the AI race

And so to really understand why Huang had to resign, why he’s being called before Congress to testify, why the SEC has reportedly launched a probe into Nvidia—you have to understand how the U.S. got locked in this AI race with China, and how Nvidia’s chips work to power the AI boom

You have to understand the policies that have led to the export restrictions on the chips that Nvidia sells, and the convoluted loopholes that Nvidia and Alice Huang have allegedly used to get chips into China
And my guest today: He not only understands every element of this story; he helps shape it
Ben Buchanan is the former White House special adviser on AI during the Biden administration
Buchanan helped design the chip-export controls on China that Huang and Nvidia lobbied against
And along with Tantum Collins, he’s the author of this new book, The Bitter Struggle: Superintelligence, Superpowers, and the Fate of the World
He was in the room for so many of the events that led to where we are now
And today, he’s going to help us mere mortals actually understand what the heck is going on with China, chips, Jensen Huang, the AI race, and crucially, why all of it matters
I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . [ Music ] Warzel: Ben Buchanan, welcome to Galaxy Brain
Warzel: So I’m hoping in this interview that we could do some very basic questions that will lead to this deeper understanding of the U.S.-China race, the labs; what’s going on
But first I just want to ask about Jensen Huang

Have you taken what we know now and reexamined any of either the interactions you’ve had with him or his company? Like, were there things in retrospect that now that look like signs of vulnerability? How are you processing this news moment, given your relationship to this entire story? Buchanan: For background, I was the White House special adviser for AI and worked in the National Security Council, and was the architect of a lot of the chip controls that seem to be at the crux of this story here
In the course of doing that work for four years, we had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia
They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that
But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration

Certainly about the importance of chips to national security, the importance of AI to national security, and the necessity to cut off smuggling routes and remote access routes for China to get access to that technology
So, in some sense, it’s like a new chapter in a long-running novel
Maybe a particularly salacious and interesting chapter
But it fits the themes of the novel that I’ve lived, I guess now for six years
And I want to get into the stuff about Megaspeed: the company that Huang’s alleged mistress, and alleged Chinese intelligence asset, worked for

Like, was all this on your radar, and you were expecting it all to come out in some fashion? Or were you pretty shocked by the fact that we’re all talking about this right now? Buchanan: I never knew of the sex thing
As best I can recall, I did not know of Megaspeed in the government
I definitely don’t think I ever heard the name Alice Huang
Megaspeed is in the book because The New York Times did a good story on it 13 or 14 months ago
And it looked to us, when we were writing the book, as a great avatar or example of exactly the kind of smuggling and remote access we were worried about, and we were trying to prevent

While the particulars of this case are new to me, or at least were not something we discussed in the government, the general idea of circumvention of the export controls because this technology is so important was something that we spent a lot of time on and in fact were actively trying to combat
Warzel: So I wanna ask some basic questions here, because I imagine I’m not alone in what is essentially like a pretty shallow understanding of the story in Nvidia
I think, you know, reading the news, a lot of people understand they make advanced AI chips, power the boom we’re experiencing here
They have an extraordinary amount of market share

title: The Benefits of Reading Are Incalculable
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
The next wellness craze is reading, my colleague Sophie Haigney reported in The Atlantic this week
She tried a new app called Readwise Books, which tracks a user’s words-per-minute the way a health app might track their mileage or heart rate
This is just one example of how influencers and the health-conscious have recently been making “a case for reading’s value that sounds a lot like the way we talk about physical health,” Haigney wrote
The fitness challenge 75 Hard, she noted, doesn’t just prescribe workouts and a specific water intake
It also requires participants to read “10 pages of nonfiction a day.” But it offers no guidance about what those titles should be or how to discern the value of any given 10-page chunk

More confusing to me was a claim, from the bodybuilder and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, that picking up books is “a low-risk behavior (really, there’s no risk in reading more).” First, here are 6 new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section: One word to explain America Welcome to the era of second-screen reading The loneliness of buying too many things The writer who made food fun “Long Wave,” a short story by Daisy Johnson “Caravaggio,” a poem by Peter Balakian That stopped me in my tracks

No risk? If Schwarzenegger, or any other literature-as-wellbeing influencer, truly believes that the activity is as powerful as they say it is, how can that be true? Written language is so central to our society because it can, and does, lead to real action

If printed matter has the potential to change stubborn minds, inspire the most unlikely empathy, and transmit the wildest human ideas, then perusing 10 pages of a hateful manifesto could, under the right circumstances, entail a lot of risk
I don’t mean to make an argument for locking away dangerous ideas or for thinking of books as vectors of unwholesome thoughts
Instead, like Haigney, I’m skeptical of anyone who posits reading as a harmless, vaguely healthful behavior akin to eating vegetables or wearing sunscreen

I think that people arguing for reading as a practice of personal and spiritual transformation should follow their premise to its conclusions: Books can alter a life, undermine foundational beliefs, even change the world
Tracking one’s reading as if it were a workout shortchanges its power
What debates over the end of literacy sometimes miss is that the content of a book is far more important than any metric—whether words-per-minute or year-over-year sales

I’ve argued this before , when I encouraged people to measure themselves not by statistics but instead by qualitative benchmarks: “Finish Anna Karenina ” is a more meaningful goal than “turn 900 pages.” Slipping and sliding across 3,200 frictionless pages of A Court of Thorns and Roses feels like a wholly different exercise than the deliberate, engaged immersion of Edward P
And neither is going to improve my VO2 max—which is fine by me, because that’s not why I’m reading them
Let’s Not Make Reading a Wellness Trend By Sophie Haigney Books have long been considered morally and intellectually virtuous
Now some influencers are claiming that they’re good for your physical health

What to Read The Invisible Kingdom , by Meghan O’Rourke The best memoirs are those that take an occurrence, a life, or a history that is not our own, and so fully transport the reader into the world of the writer that our capacity for empathy expands in ways we could not have imagined
That is the experience I had reading O’Rourke’s The Invisible Kingdom , in which she writes beautifully and honestly about living with a chronic, mysterious, and often debilitating illness
Some of my loved ones live with their own enigmatic, ongoing health issues, and this book provided me with insight and context with which to more fully understand their experiences
O’Rourke places her life in conversation with the larger body of historical research on chronic illness, to provide a narrative that is both deeply personal and deeply investigated

In the age of COVID, when so many across the world are still living with the lingering, enervating symptoms of the virus, the lessons and stories here are becoming more relevant to all of us—just as they were for me. — Clint Smith From our list: A book that changed how I think Out Next Week 📚 Long Wave , by Daisy Johnson 📚 Arlington: An African American History , by William A

Blair 📚 Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir , by Bob Woodward Your Weekend Read Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic The Least Productive Day of the Year By Sophia Nguyen Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off
First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up
But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19
Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas
She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out

title: The Taylor Swift Museum Exhibition Is an SOS Call
excerpt: When the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, shared Tuesday that it would mount an exhibition of Taylor Swift costumes, instruments, and other objects next year, the p
body: When the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, shared Tuesday that it would mount an exhibition of Taylor Swift costumes, instruments, and other objects next year, the public response seemed to fall into two camps
Swifties were thrilled, and art purists criticized the museum for succumbing to visitor bait

But really, neither scorn nor celebration is the right response to a show that one of the museum’s curators describes as representing “a remarkable musical journey across genres over the last 20 years.” A 156-year-old institution raiding a pop star’s closet should be seen for what it is: a cry for help
The show does not entirely flout museum norms
The MFA’s collection includes fashion and musical instruments

Art institutions have examined celebrity wardrobes in the past (see the landmark David Bowie exhibition that traveled around the world), and museums frequently highlight living visual artists and designers—sometimes, as in the Met’s recent plans for a John Galliano exhibit, to their peril
Why not Swift? She seems to have conquered nearly every other corner of the culture
An illustration of her range: She both is the subject of university courses and once had her own special-edition ketchup bottle
Perhaps to her fans, her rightful place in history is alongside the old masters and the Impressionists
Step back, and you can see why there’s hype for the show, but it’s still a mismatch
The museum sector has been having a hard time lately, making this type of pop-culture play understandably tempting
But after the MFA laid off 33 employees, including curators of Islamic art, Native American art, and fashion arts, earlier this year, the show choice looks more than a little desperate

Although Taylor Swift’s sartorial history may be worthy of serious scholarly analysis—mass culture certainly has a place in art museums, which should help us understand the visual world writ large—tackling the subject of a living celebrity at the height of her fame renders hagiography practically a foregone conclusion
The MFA is not even pretending otherwise: One staffer made a point of extending a special welcome to Swifties in the announcement
The exhibition will very likely serve as an advertisement for a star who needs no such boost in the hopes that the museum can lure more visitors, who will be paying $40 each to look at her stuff
For an institution that contains one of the finest art collections in the world, the decision belies a deep insecurity

When I saw the news, I had an urge to shout at the MFA like it’s a friend of mine who’s in a toxic relationship: You don’t need her, buddy! You’re great! The tendency to star-cast museum shows does not necessarily lead to bad or uninteresting results

These exhibitions have historically taken one of two approaches: In one, the celebrity might be drafted to curate an exhibition (which must be a tad annoying to the curators who might’ve gone through the trouble of getting a degree to do that)
In the other, the museum assembles an exhibit of the celebrity’s belongings or artistic ephemera
The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which went through its own round of layoffs last year, recently opened an exhibition doing a bit of both
The institution is currently showcasing nearly 150 works from the art collection of the BTS member RM, and the show is co-curated by the K-pop star himself
Some celebrity-infused endeavors have succeeded, such as the acclaimed Bowie show or a well-liked exhibition of Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz’s collection that the Brooklyn Museum organized

Others, such as Björk at the Museum of Modern Art in 2015 or the Pablo Picasso show co-curated by Hannah Gadsby at the Brooklyn Museum in 2023, flopped with critics but drew crowds, presumably fulfilling their purpose
If it’s not clear, I am neither a Swiftie nor a K-pop stan, which may disqualify me from a conversation for the truly devout

That said, having lived in Seoul, I am a real admirer of Korean art and would accept almost any strategy to show more Americans Kim Whanki’s moving abstractions or Chang Ucchin’s charming pastoral scenes
And the RM exhibit has done that, breaking museum records
Such shows can raise ethical questions—displaying any person’s art collection, for example, can inflate its value—but more than that, they can hurt a museum’s credibility

A doctor would not hand her sutures over to Beyoncé just because her surgery numbers are down, nor would a losing football team throw Justin Bieber on the field because he might bring in some new fans
The stakes are different in museums, but these places shape history, care for cultural heritage, and at their core, are meant to challenge and educate visitors
The stakes of swapping in celebrities for curators and their paraphernalia for objects are not exactly low either
Many museums have struggled to rebound after the pandemic changed visitor habits and have not found their way in a world that seems to become more digital by the day
They’ve faced alternating allegations of being overly woke and being complicit in colonialism
And although they are widely trusted , museums remain one of the few places that spark anxiety among would-be visitors over not having done their homework
No one hesitates to go to a concert because they didn’t study music theory
Perhaps you cannot blame the MFA or SFMOMA for looking to the crowd-pleaser to pad the numbers

Paying the bills, for the MFA, might mean loosening up a bit—not everyone wants to parse the stories told by an intricate Japanese folding screen or sit long enough with a Mondrian to see how it’s more than just a colorful grid
But museums’ usual purview holds plenty of mass appeal as is

In a way, the situation parallels how museums tap certain go-to artists and genres to woo the public: Yayoi Kusama with her impossibly photogenic mirrors; Impressionists with their coffee-table-book-ready textural landscapes; the treasures of ancient Egypt
The best museums don’t just give people what they want, though; they teach us how to look, and empower us to find aesthetic joy for ourselves
More compelling than celebrity shows are efforts to pull new audiences that confidently lean into what museums already do

title: The Old-School Dating Ritual People Can’t Seem to Shake
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter

A man and woman leave a restaurant. “I had a nice time—” she begins, but he’s already off, skateboarding away with nothing more than a “Call me.” Then she receives a Venmo request: “your half.” Out pops the actor Julia Fox, here to impart a warning

She shows a montage of how a relationship might unfold with this scruffy, nonchalant man—flashes of him playing video games in a filthy apartment, holding an umbrella over himself while she gets drenched, presenting her with a cheap engagement ring
The message is clear: If he won’t pay for your dinner now, he’ll be a stingy, unchivalrous man-child forever

It’s for the new “Anti 50/50 Campaign” she’s promoting with the dating site Seeking, which involves a $50,000 fund to reimburse singles who have split the check on a date (up to $50 a person). “Seeking is challenging what it sees as a decline in generosity,” the press release reads

In the company’s own survey, 75 percent of women said they prefer men to “take the lead on dates,” including planning and paying—yet 61 percent of female Zoomers said they’ve been asked to share the bill

Seeking regards this as an affront to straight women everywhere. “I’m all for women being independent,” Fox says in the release, “but that doesn’t mean we have to entertain low-effort men who think splitting a check is the height of romance
If you’re going to court somebody, COURT THEM.” Of all the causes Fox could take up in our year 2026, this one is oddly old-fashioned

But Seeking is taking advantage of something real: The expectation that men should foot the bill, especially on the first date, is still stubbornly ubiquitous , even among women who see themselves as progressive or critical of strict gender norms
In a dating world that can feel hard and confusing, many singles are looking for explicit rules—and many straight women are looking for a man who offers care and consistency

Alas, a paid check does not a gentleman make. [ Read: Bumble moves the first move back to men ] The bill-paying convention, like it or not, has its roots in a philosophy of clear-cut gender difference: Men are born providers and leaders, whereas women are passive and dependent
For many years, this was the logic by which American society generally operated
Women had precious few career opportunities; their presumed job was to be a wife and mother
So in the early 20th century, when more women began dating in public spaces rather than having suitors visit their home, men were expected to pay
Now, though, a far greater number of women are financially self-sufficient
In this context, the assumption that men should pay for dates seems a bit weird, and weirdly pervasive

For her 2020 book, The Mating Game: How Gender Still Shapes How We Date , the Appalachian State University sociologist Ellen Lamont interviewed college-educated young adults and found that more than two-thirds of women participants said that all of their first dates were covered by the man
Many of them would offer to split the check as a test, hoping that the man would insist on paying

One 27-year-old told Lamont that she didn’t find it important for a man to grab the first check, but “I would expect it, and then if he expected me to pay for half, or if he expected me to pay, then I’d be like, I’m out .” So it was important, then? Lamont clarified. “I guess it is,” the woman conceded. “’Cause I’d be like, man, he didn’t even pay, what a douche.” Lamont has found that courtship norms are unusually sticky
Many people dismiss the idea of stark, inherent gender differences in other realms—they think that women are just as equipped as men to have a career, or that men should be equally involved parents
Yet at the same time, they quietly maintain that men should be the ones to ask women out, pay for dates, suggest exclusivity or commitment, and propose marriage

People are motivated by their own interests, after all; women fought for the right to vote and to enter the workforce not just for the abstract concept of equality but also because they wanted a say and a paycheck
A woman might find splitting the bill about as appealing as a man might view splitting the housework
And guidelines can be comforting, especially for a ritual as intimidating as dating
So people tend to follow the rules—even rules they don’t fully stand behind in theory

Some people have told me that men should get the tab because they make more money on average. (If this was really the logic, shouldn’t the higher-earning person pay, whoever it may be?) Others—including some men I’ve spoken with—hold that the least men can do is front the bill, given that the woman otherwise tends to bring more to the table: better listening skills, empathy, social graces
The man, according to this line of thinking, is lucky to be there at all, whereas the woman has more to lose—especially in a climate of misogyny and prevalent harassment
But putting women on such a pedestal, presuming that they’re inherently soft and nurturing and pulled together, is flattening in its own way

Many women also see willingness to pay as a sign of genuine interest: “an easy gimme,” Lamont said, particularly for young women who have recently left college hookup culture behind and are looking for courtship that feels serious and grown-up
Regardless of gender, reading someone’s feelings is difficult
And a lot of women look for tokens of dedication, she said, because they’ve been told again and again that men are commitment-phobic libertines
Something as prosaic as a credit card in a cup, when you’re scanning for green flags, can take on outsize significance
This was true at the time of Lamont’s research, and it may be even truer now, when a lot of straight women are fed up with a perceived lack of enthusiasm from male prospects

The dating app Bumble, once known for its “women message first” policy, now allows men to initiate; when the company surveyed women, it found that many were tired of putting themselves out there and wanted men to step up—to be present, active, eager

Meanwhile, a slew of think pieces have captured a similar yearning. “Lately I have been bruised by the ambivalence of men,” the writer Jean Garnett wrote in The New York Times , recalling a man who’d canceled their date when he was feeling anxious. “Where were the men who could handle hard stuff? Like leaving the house for sex?” The headline of another Times story summed up the sentiment: “Men, Where Have You Gone? Please Come Back.” The problem is that bill paying alone isn’t actually a good gauge of emotional investment
Many of the men Lamont interviewed told her that they’d grab the check even when they had no interest in seeing their date again

A man can also be rich, keen, and a self-involved jerk. (A 2016 study of university students in California found that, among male participants, embracing traditional courtship norms was associated with “hostile sexism” and the disavowal of feminism.) On the flip side, a man who suggests splitting the bill might be earnestly trying to foster an equitable dynamic
Or maybe he just doesn’t have the money to throw down $100 every time he takes someone out, and maybe—going out on a limb here—being broke doesn’t make someone a lazy schlub
A ton of single people today, men and women alike, say they’re forgoing dating because it’s too expensive

The team behind Seeking understands this on some level; the company refers to “rising dating costs and growing frustration with the modern dating experience” as its raison d’être—but it seems to find that strain to be a problem for only half the population

title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
excerpt: AI keeps getting faster at verifiable tasks — METR's updated report confirms that frontier AI models are doubling their performance on measurable tasks eve
body: AI keeps getting faster at verifiable tasks — METR's updated report confirms that frontier AI models are doubling their performance on measurable tasks every four months
Judgment is where models still stumble — When asked to design new AI evaluations or score philosophical arguments, even the most advanced models fell short of human performance

Some glimmers of progress, but no clean trend lines — A handful of newer models are now scoring "borderline above the bar" on evaluation design tasks, up from "clearly below" just a year ago — though researchers warn these improvements are too sparse to predict where things are headed. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149399" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding
The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used
METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans
Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete
That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled
The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended

One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure

We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures
That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work
It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction
For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them
But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development
And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now

Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two

That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement
METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development
In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results

Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research
In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments
This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D
On this task, too, models fell short of human performance

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own

And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite
Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says

Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well

And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better
Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising
Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D

METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming

Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual
It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming
It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment

And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says
But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death
In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars
In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas
After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck
Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?” Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.” It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.” There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet
I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.” To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand

title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
url:
<title>Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773223/original/file-20261120-62-73fv9n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5168%2C3445&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A &#39;Saturday Night Live&#39; parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-hugging-her-elderly-mother-royalty-free-image/1915738426?adppopup=true"> Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/health/wellness/snl-sister-caregiving-skit-3a6043e4?mod=wknd_pos1">hit home for a lot of people</a>.</p>

<p>The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.</p>

<p>“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.</p>

<p>I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-daunting-economics-of-elder-care-are-about-to-get-much-worse-83123">daunting economics of caregiving for older adults</a> for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.</p>



<h2>A growing trend</h2>

<p>One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.</p>

<p>My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That <a href="https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/ppi/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-us-2025.doi.10.26419-2fppi.00373.001.pdf">number has since risen to 63 million</a> – about 1 in 4 adults.</p>

<p>The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/valuing-the-invaluable-2026-update/">estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/-X9dxL17t1k?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down</h2>

<p>Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.</p>

<p>Caregiving is tough work, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/01.NAJ.0000336406.45248.4c">numerous studies over the years</a> have found that <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/family-caregivers-health-well-being/">caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress</a> than other people.</p>

<p>That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”</p>

<h2>Family caregivers pay a price</h2>

<p>Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of <a href="https://health.usnews.com/home-care/articles/how-much-do-in-home-caregivers-cost">in-home care is $35 per hour</a>, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MEHOINUSA646N">median annual household income of $87,460</a>. </p>

<p>But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.</p>

<p>Over <a href="https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/ppi/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/hidden-cost-caregiving-lost-earnings-retirement-income-social-security-income.doi.10.26419-2fppi.00433.001.pdf">90% of caregivers must cut their work hours</a>), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. </p>

<p>Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.</p>

<p>AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C15%2C1900%2C1068&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A women with dark hair holds a phone to her ear while sitting in front of a table with prescription bottles." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C15%2C1900%2C1068&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=437&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">NBC</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A ‘daughterhood penalty’</h2>

<p>Sociologists have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122416686521">men with a sister do less parental caregiving</a> than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “<a href="https://www.pbs.org/video/the-daughterhood-penalty-in-americas-caregiving-crisis-qa1c2g/">daughterhood penalty</a>,” or tax. </p>

<p>Social psychologists <a href="https://direct.mit.edu/daed/article/154/1/82/127938/Why-Do-Women-Care-More-amp-Men-Couldn-t-Care-Less">Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught</a> that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.</p>

<p><a href="https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/gender-norms-and-labour-market">Economists’ explanations of gender differences</a> in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, <a href="https://www.proquest.com/openview/6d8960e654bbfcf09490b30f225ac591/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&amp;cbl=1059">economists like me</a> also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.</p>

<p>But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.</p>

<p>Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-024-11191-w">three times more time doing household chores</a> than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297041/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party. </span></em></p></content>

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid
And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity
That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion
The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving
Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes
That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes
But their freedom to age in place comes at a price
Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families
The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care
Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460
But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones
Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits
Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving

Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members
NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister
They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother
This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability
Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience

Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives
But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024
This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores

<title>‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773179/original/file-20261119-62-z1etq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=124%2C0%2C1650%2C1100&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A recent &#39;SNL&#39; sketch called &#39;Sister&#39; lampoons gender roles in caring for aging parents. </span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">NBC</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-X9dxL17t1k">Sister</a>” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?</p>

<p>The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.</p>

<p>According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-the-us-2025/">63 million Americans provide ongoing care</a> to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YV7PMrEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">researchers</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=WmF6WoIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">who study aging</a>, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/gnaf011">initially have better health and financial status</a> than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.</p>

<p>While societal gender expectations help explain why <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/upshot/sister-snl-elder-care.html">daughters often assume the bulk</a> of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/-X9dxL17t1k?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch immediately went viral.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care</h2>

<p>One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/long-term-care">generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance</a> with everyday activities.</p>

<p>Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/home-health-services">Medicare’s home health benefit</a>, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets <a href="https://www.cms.gov/training-education/medicare-learning-networkr-mln/compliance/medicare-provider-compliance-tips/home-health-services">Medicare’s homebound requirements</a>.</p>

<p>This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.71345">national median cost of a home health aide</a> was approximately US$6,688 per month, while <a href="https://www.oasissenioradvisors.com/what-assisted-living/">residing in an assisted living facility</a> averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.</p>

<p>For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that <a href="https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/dual-burden-housing-and-care-older-adults">76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance</a> from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.</p>



<h2>Medicaid can help, but access is limited</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/long-term-services-supports">Medicaid</a>, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.</p>

<p>Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-home-care-hcbs-in-2025/">covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023</a>. The <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/long-term-care-in-the-united-states-a-timeline">divide between these programs dates back to 1965</a>, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.</p>

<p>However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.</p>

<p>Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-look-at-waiting-lists-for-medicaid-home-and-community-based-services-from-2016-to-2026/">spend more than a year on waitlists to get services</a>.</p>

<p>Who provides care in the meantime?</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C318%2C6103%2C3432&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An adult daughter helps her mother walk down a ramp." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C318%2C6103%2C3432&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773087/original/file-20261119-64-6fpi6l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">As the sketch suggests, daughters are more likely to care for their aging parents.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/senior-headed-down-ramp-to-car-royalty-free-image/2236946401?phrase=daughter%20caregiver&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Visual Vic/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>There’s a shortage of paid caregivers</h2>

<p>Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling <a href="https://kffhealthnews.org/aging/dying-broke-why-long-term-care-insurance-falls-short/">options available through private insurers</a> to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.</p>

<p>The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – <a href="https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/recent-immigration-policies-threaten-sustainability-ltss-workforce">one-third of these workers are foreign-born</a>.</p>

<p>The median hourly wage for <a href="https://www.phinational.org/resource/direct-care-workers-in-the-united-states-key-facts-2026/">direct care work was $17.99 in 2025</a>, only <a href="https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-fast-food-wages-in-every-u-s-state/">$2-$3 per hour</a> more than what fast-food workers earned. </p>

<h2>Caregiving often has financial consequences</h2>

<p>When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.</p>

<p>Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only <a href="https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/ltss/family-caregiving/caregiving-in-the-us-2025/">reduce their income</a> right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.</p>

<p>The federal <a href="https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fmla/family-caregiver">Family and Medical Leave Act</a> provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.</p>

<p>Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.</p>

<h2>Families often have to shoulder responsibility</h2>

<p>Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/state-paid-family-leave-laws-across-the-u-s/">dozen other states</a>, for example, have launched <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0009.12708">paid family leave programs</a>. In <a href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaids-home-care-support-for-family-caregivers-in-2025/">New York and some other states</a> Medicaid is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/haschl/qxaf192">compensating family caregivers</a>. Washington state is helping <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0009.12439">finance long-term care coverage</a>.</p>

<p>In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris <a href="https://theconversation.com/harris-proposes-that-medicare-cover-more-in-home-health-care-filling-a-large-gap-for-older-americans-and-their-caregivers-240865">proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance</a>, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.</p>



<p>“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.</p>

<p>When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297022/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’
