<title>Trump administration may fund white South Africans to document ‘hateful rhetoric and violent acts’</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772571/original/file-20261117-78-96a176.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6720%2C4480&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">South Africans prepare to join a convoy in October 2025 to a memorial for white farmers who were victims of violent crimes.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/farmers-prepare-to-drive-in-a-convoy-to-a-memorial-for-news-photo/2239179684?adppopup=true">Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The U.S. State Department <a href="https://www.sabcnews.com/sabcnews/trump-administrations-looks-to-award-near-1m-to-afriforum/">will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum</a>, a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa.</p>

<p>The grant, first <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/afriforum-grant-trump-white-south-africans">reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026</a>, would support research to document the “<a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/bureau-of-democracy-human-rights-and-labor/2026/08/documentation-of-hateful-rhetoric-targeting-minority-populations-in-south-africa">hateful rhetoric and violent acts</a>” experienced by <a href="https://www.nprillinois.org/2025-11-20/who-are-afrikaners-the-group-at-the-center-of-trumps-dispute-with-south-africa">Afrikaners</a> – <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-trumps-claims-of-white-farmer-genocide-in-south-africa">descendants of white Dutch settlers</a> who moved to South Africa in the 17th century.</p>

<p>As scholars who study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=a8EwKzoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">foreign aid</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VYsdAEIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">civil society organizations</a>, we would see U.S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs <a href="https://www.ned.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2025-Annual-Report.pdf">the U.S. has funded in the past</a>.</p>



<h2>Supporting democracy by funding NGOs</h2>

<p>The U.S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and <a href="https://2021-2025.state.gov/u-s-achievements-in-advancing-human-rights-globally/">strengthen human rights protections</a>. </p>

<p>Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U.S. Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy. </p>

<p>Past administrations called this assistance “<a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12523">fundamental</a>” to the goals of U.S. foreign policy. By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost <a href="https://dx.doi.org/10.1353/sais.2026.a1000457">$3 billion annually</a>.</p>

<p>Some of this money has <a href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/09/29/fact-sheet-us-support-civil-society">supported NGOs engaged</a> in civic participation and media independence. These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where <a href="https://www.ssoar.info/ssoar/bitstream/handle/document/113371/ssoar-2026-gessner_et_al-Backsliding_Democracy_The_Crisis_for.pdf">civil society is especially at risk</a>.</p>

<p>NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups. By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/pad.1995">stave off future violence</a>.</p>

<h2>Slashing foreign aid</h2>

<p>The Trump administration suspended most <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/reevaluating-and-realigning-united-states-foreign-aid/">U.S. foreign aid in January 2025</a>, soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time.</p>

<p>It then <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/07/01/nx-s1-5451372/usaid-officially-shuts-down-and-merges-remaining-operations-with-state-department">dismantled USAID</a>, the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/07/18/nx-s1-5469912/npr-congress-rescission-funding-trumpe">rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending</a>. It has continued to take steps in that direction with or <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/14/world/trump-administration-foreign-aid-global-health-diverted-intl">without lawmakers’ cooperation</a>.</p>

<p>As a result, many <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Into-the-Wood-Chipper/Nicholas-Enrich/9781668226957">lifesaving public health programs</a> lost funding. This policy change has had an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(25)01186-9">enormous human toll</a>, which public health <a href="https://www.impactcounter.com/dashboard?view=table&amp;sort=title&amp;order=asc">researchers have begun to quantify</a>.   </p>

<p>In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut. <a href="https://carnegieendowment.org/research/2025/03/does-us-democracy-aid-have-a-future">USAID’s Democracy Fund</a>, which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated. The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/05/29/rubio-human-rights-state-00374606">funding and staffing</a> for <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R49019/R49019.3.pdf">promoting democracy were also slashed</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="President Trump holds a meeting in the Oval Office with a lot of people crowded around." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772570/original/file-20261117-64-7irw9i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">U.S. President Donald Trump presents printed news articles to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office in May 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/may-21-2025-us-president-donald-trump-presents-printed-news-news-photo/2215854564?phrase=south%2Bafrica%2Bcyril%2Btrump">Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Claiming there’s a ‘white genocide’</h2>

<p>In our research on NGOs that work on promoting democracy and the prevention of violence, we have seen and documented the <a href="https://ssir.org/articles/entry/preventing-identity-based-violence-in-conflict-zones">benefits of these efforts</a>. The organizations we have studied emphasize how people in South Africa and other countries with a history of identity-based violence can learn to live together across racial, ethnic and religious divides.  </p>

<p>By contrast, <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/afriforum-grant-trump-white-south-africans">AfriForum seeks to lift up Afrikaner identity and history</a>, <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/us-and-foreign-governments-should-be-skeptical-afriforums-lobbying">without any evident effort</a> to bridge the divide between Afrikaners and other racial groups in South Africa. </p>

<p>It champions causes that have contributed to what South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, scholars and other analysts call a false narrative of a “<a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpos.2026.1886481">white genocide</a>” in that country.</p>

<p>In fact, researchers have found that Afrikaners and other white people in South Africa are less likely to be <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cgr5xe7z0y0o">victims of crime</a> and <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cgr5xe7z0y0o">other forms of violence</a> compared to other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa. </p>

<p>By funding AfriForum, the State Department would be elevating the <a href="https://theconversation.com/trump-and-south-africa-what-is-white-victimhood-and-how-is-it-linked-to-white-supremacy-249648">dubious claims the group makes</a> about the oppression of Afrikaners in South Africa.</p>

<p>And <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-american-fixation-on-white-afrikaners-in-south-africa-stretches-back-nearly-a-century-270145">the Trump administration’s embrace</a> of this false narrative goes beyond this grant for AfriForum. It explains why the U.S. has <a href="https://za.usembassy.gov/refugee-admissions-program-for-south-africans/">allowed thousands of white South Africans</a> to come to the U.S. as refugees while denying admission to <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF13277">nearly all other refugees</a> from the rest of the world.</p>

State Department will reportedly give US$1 million to AfriForum , a nongovernmental organization that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners in South Africa

The grant, first reported by ProPublica on Nov. 5, 2026 , would support research to document the “ hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” experienced by Afrikaners – descendants of white Dutch settlers who moved to South Africa in the 17th century
As scholars who study foreign aid and civil society organizations , we would see U.S. support for AfriForum as a radical departure from the kinds of NGOs the U.S. has funded in the past
Supporting democracy by funding NGOs The U.S. used foreign aid for decades to support efforts to build democracy abroad, enhance governance and strengthen human rights protections
Until the second Trump administration, the primary government agencies distributing this assistance were the U.S
Agency for International Development, the State Department and the National Endowment for Democracy
Past administrations called this assistance “ fundamental ” to the goals of U.S. foreign policy
By the end of President Joe Biden’s term, funding for democracy promotion had reached almost $3 billion annually
Some of this money has supported NGOs engaged in civic participation and media independence
These efforts had been particularly important in fragile states and fledgling democracies, where civil society is especially at risk
NGOs can also play an important role in reducing risks of violence between different ethnic and religious groups
By raising awareness about past atrocities, they can help stave off future violence
Slashing foreign aid The Trump administration suspended most U.S. foreign aid in January 2025 , soon after Donald Trump was sworn in as president for a second time

It then dismantled USAID , the federal agency previously responsible for foreign aid and development assistance, and the White House compelled Congress to rescind billions of dollars of foreign aid spending
It has continued to take steps in that direction with or without lawmakers’ cooperation
As a result, many lifesaving public health programs lost funding
This policy change has had an enormous human toll , which public health researchers have begun to quantify
In addition, democracy assistance has been severely cut
USAID’s Democracy Fund , which funded programs dedicated to building democratic institutions and promoting fair elections and respect for human rights, was eliminated
The Department of State’s and National Endowment for Democracy’s funding and staffing for promoting democracy were also slashed

<title>Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768396/original/file-20261026-52-dks93m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=180%2C0%2C1948%2C1298&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Kierkegaard may be known for writings on religion and existentialism, but he had plenty to say about love.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/crumpled-red-paper-heart-isolated-on-white-royalty-free-image/2186261940?phrase=love%20crush&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Helen Slyvinska/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.</p>

<p>It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/therapists/ross-channing-reed-salem-mo/819017">As a counselor</a>, I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And <a href="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ross-channing-reed-2329706">as a philosopher</a>, I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/collected-works/collected-soren-kierkegaard?srsltid=AU7gw4XM6tLn-3Smw2n773iteBLewhcvrdq_GVaI8qFNbvF36X5QE-l6">Søren Kierkegaard</a> to reflect on <a href="https://philpapers.org/rec/REELAA">the differences</a> <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/precarity-trauma-addiction-and-love-in-philosophical-counseling-9781666934373/">between the two</a>.</p>

<p>Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the <a href="https://www.issep.org/features/death-meaning-kierkegaard">father of existentialism</a>, which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/love-reason-and-will-9781628927320/">love is a central focus</a> of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.</p>

<h2>Aesthetic love</h2>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A painting in dark colors shows a man with thick hair reading papers at a slanted desk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=858&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=858&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=858&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1078&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1078&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769311/original/file-20261030-78-l9ipdp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1078&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A painting of philosopher Søren Kierkegaard made several years after his death by Danish artist Luplau Janssen.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kierkegaard_1902_by_Luplau_Janssen.jpg">The Museum of National History at Frederiksborg Castle via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/kierkegaards-eitheror/BE26EB1A66389A26B4CD4D414A21BF2A#fndtn-information">his first book of philosophy</a> – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.</p>

<p>“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “<a href="https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.187782/2015.187782.Either---Or-volume-One_djvu.txt">aesthetic</a>” and “<a href="https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.504967/page/n7/mode/2up">ethical</a>” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.</p>

<p>Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” <a href="https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.187782/2015.187782.Either---Or-volume-One_djvu.txt">Kierkegaard wrote</a>.</p>

<p>Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love <a href="https://dn760100.eu.archive.org/0/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.187384/2015.187384.Works-Of-Love.pdf">lacks the trust and respect</a> needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511487736">is centered on feelings and desires</a>, not principles.</p>

<p>Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.</p>

<p>A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world. </p>

<p>This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it <a href="https://philpapers.org/rec/REELAA">similar to addiction</a>: a pattern that <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691253534/what-would-you-do-alone-in-a-cage-with-nothing-but-cocaine?srsltid=AU7gw4X6jIw51M9OJtHZE-yMTgghGU8pMDuFrdC_dlC0M2ZHvwE-X21N">we feel compelled to continue</a>, despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. <a href="https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-responsibility-empirical/">Psychologists</a> <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10151124/#ref-179368">and philosophers</a> <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/article/652207">debate</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/16066359.2018.1543412">how to define “addiction</a>,” and <a href="https://www.therapistsinprovidence.com/therapy-insights-blog/is-love-addiction-real-understanding-problematic-relationship-patterns-providence">whether love can become one</a>, but <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00687">research indicates</a> there can be <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3134413/#S5">similarities in behavior</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00213-012-2794-x">brain activity</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01436">between the two</a>.</p>

<p>Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man with salt-and-pepper hair puts his head in his hands as he sits on a couch, about a foot away from a woman staring into space." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768399/original/file-20261026-52-mmfq0f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A bad relationship can hurt both people, but often neither wants to give it up.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/man-doing-a-desperate-gesture-during-couples-royalty-free-image/1369572239?phrase=couple%27s%20counseling&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Carles Navarro Parcerisas/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “<a href="https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.187782/2015.187782.Either---Or-volume-One_djvu.txt">a kind of despair</a>,” rooted in <a href="https://ia601400.us.archive.org/32/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.189042/2015.189042.The-Sickness-Unto-Death_text.pdf">estrangement from oneself</a>, a kind of self-rejection or self-deception. </p>

<p>Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love <a href="https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.504967/page/n3/mode/2up">seeks freedom</a> through the other person, rather than freely loving them.</p>

<h2>Ethical love</h2>

<p>For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “<a href="https://archive.org/details/eitherorvolumeii0000sren">Either/Or</a>” and in “<a href="https://dn760100.eu.archive.org/0/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.187384/2015.187384.Works-Of-Love.pdf">Works of Love</a>,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.</p>

<p>Kierkegaard maintains that <a href="https://dn760100.eu.archive.org/0/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.187384/2015.187384.Works-Of-Love.pdf">ethical love</a> lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.</p>

<p>Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, <a href="https://dn721908.ca.archive.org/0/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.187384/2015.187384.Works-Of-Love.pdf">Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love</a>.”</p>

<p>It should be based on respect: <a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/I-And-Thou/Martin-Buber/9780684717258">treating other people as ends</a> in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, <a href="https://ia801900.us.archive.org/7/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.187384/2015.187384.Works-Of-Love.pdf">ethical love</a> is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.</p>

<p>Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/243464">he wrote</a>.</p>

<p>This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to <a href="https://ia601400.us.archive.org/32/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.189042/2015.189042.The-Sickness-Unto-Death_text.pdf">become ourselves</a>, a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God. </p>

<p>Kierkegaard stresses that <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/243464">ethical love liberates</a> not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.</p>

<p>The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291950/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Kierkegaard may be known for writings on religion and existentialism, but he had plenty to say about love
Helen Slyvinska/iStock via Getty Images Plus Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular
You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight
It’s the start of many happy love stories
But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful
You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it
The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck
As a counselor , I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love
And as a philosopher , I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two
Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion
Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism , which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility
It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work
What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it
Aesthetic love A painting of philosopher Søren Kierkegaard made several years after his death by Danish artist Luplau Janssen
The Museum of National History at Frederiksborg Castle via Wikimedia Commons In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important

The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life. “Either/Or” makes a distinction between “ aesthetic ” and “ ethical ” ways of living
The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others
Each way of life has its own form of love
Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into
It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force
The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote
But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability
The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires , not principles
Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love
It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up
A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love
The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced
Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months
He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later
He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world
This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion
In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction : a pattern that we feel compelled to continue , despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us
Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction ,” and whether love can become one , but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two
Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues
He or she may seem besotted with their beloved
In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires
A bad relationship can hurt both people, but often neither wants to give it up

Carles Navarro Parcerisas/Moment via Getty Images At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “ a kind of despair ,” rooted in estrangement from oneself , a kind of self-rejection or self-deception
Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness
Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them

<title>El Niño created a skiers’ paradise in Chile – now it’s Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies’ turn</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772003/original/file-20261114-64-x38ef0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6192%2C4128&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Skiers enjoyed a long snow season in Chile&#39;s Andes Mountains in 2026, suggesting a snowy El Niño winter for parts of the U.S., too.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/skiers-ride-a-chairlift-at-the-valle-nevado-ski-resort-in-news-photo/2302261913?phrase=chile%20snow&amp;adppopup=true">Rodrigo Arangua/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>El Niño has a reputation for being a skier’s dream, <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/featured-images/snow-during-el-ni%C3%B1os-1950-2009">bringing lots of snow</a> to California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as <a href="https://www.sfgate.com/renotahoe/article/tahoe-ski-resorts-open-early-22540208.php">several feet of snow fell</a> and some resorts <a href="https://www.powder.com/news/sugar-bowl-to-open-early">prepared to open early for the season</a>. But El Niño’s supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.</p>

<p>I’m an avid skier and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=p4UqsX0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">snow scientist</a> at Colorado State University. As the U.S. snow season begins amid what’s forecast to be <a href="https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/enso/current/">one of the strongest El Niños on record</a>, let’s take a look at what Chile’s very snowy winter might tell North America about what’s to come.</p>

<h2>The pros and cons of all that precipitation</h2>

<p>El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">raises global temperatures and shifts weather patterns</a> around the world.</p>

<p>It is defined by rising surface temperatures in the east-central tropical Pacific Ocean. When temperatures there are at least <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/explore/el-nino/">0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 Fahrenheit) warmer than average</a> for three months, the world is in El Niño. The August-October average was <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/oni/v6/">2.5 C warmer (36.5 F</a>, making this among the warmest periods on record going back to 1950.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Image showing red streak out from South America to the center of the tropical Pacific Ocean" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=303&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=303&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=303&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771935/original/file-20261113-64-6oyg5w.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">During El Niños, average relative sea surface temperatures in the eastern tropical Pacific rise. That warmth affects weather patterns around the world. The image shows sea surface temperatures in October 2026 compared with the 1991-2020 average.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/figure01.gif">NOAA OISSTv2.1</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the U.S., the southern half of the country tends to be wetter than usual during strong El Niños. That happens because the Pacific jet stream shifts southward, steering storms with it. The northern tier of the U.S. tends to be drier and warmer than normal.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two maps showing snow in the Sierra Nevada in California near the Nevada border and in the Southwest, particularly the southern Rockies." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=679&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=679&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=679&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=854&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=854&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771925/original/file-20261113-64-ne56qd.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=854&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Maps show annual snowfall during the 10 strongest El Niño winters in the U.S. from 1950 to 2009 compared with the average, top, and all El Niño winters over that period. They show above-average snow in the Sierra Nevada and southern and central Rockies.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/featured-images/snow-during-el-ni%C3%B1os-1950-2009">NOAA Climate.gov</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>That pattern is almost exactly what’s being <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/long_range/seasonal.php?lead=3">forecast for the U.S. winter of 2026-27</a>. It’s also what the U.S. Southwest is already experiencing – to the extreme.</p>

<p>Powerful storms supercharged by El Niño in October and November caused widespread <a href="https://apnews.com/article/sedona-arizona-pagosa-springs-colorado-southwest-flooding-bb4bb89daf78484fb97496dfd88c4a10">destructive flooding</a> in the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=toGVKoxW7O0.">Fast-melting snow</a> and days of heavy <a href="https://climate.colostate.edu/blog/index.php/2026/10/30/one-of-the-most-extreme-rainstorms-in-state-records/">rain flooded</a> the San Juan River and Rio Grande, damaging hundreds of homes.</p>

<p><iframe id="VQY0F" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VQY0F/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Stream flow on the Rio Grande shows the amount of rainfall in 2026 compared with the rest of this century so far."></iframe></p>

<h2>Recovering from last year’s snow drought</h2>

<p>Community water systems and farms across the West need that precipitation after last winter delivered <a href="https://theconversation.com/winters-alarmingly-low-snowpack-offers-a-glimpse-of-the-changing-rhythm-of-water-in-the-western-us-279664">one of the lowest snow years</a> on record for almost the entire western United States.</p>

<p>Major reservoirs in the Colorado River basin <a href="https://www.usbr.gov/lc/riverops.html">dropped during the year to their lowest levels since they were first filled</a>. The two biggest – <a href="https://www.lakepowellwaterlevel.com/blog/lake-powell-water-level-history">Lake Powell</a> and <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/07/climate/lake-mead-record-low-water-level-colorado-river">Lake Mead</a> – together supply water for <a href="https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-the-two-largest-reservoirs-in-the-us-have-hit-record-low-levels">about 40 million people</a> and hydropower for hundreds of thousands of people.</p>

<p><iframe id="tSPSb" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/tSPSb/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Lake Powell's water storage"></iframe></p>

<p>The very low snowfall, as well as <a href="https://www.weather.gov/pub/Climate2026WinterReviewSpringPreview">unusually warm midwinter temperatures</a> that <a href="https://doi.org/10.64628/AAI.3fu3dm36y">drove sublimation</a> – the evaporation of snow – reduced water stored in the mountains. And that was followed by <a href="https://coyotegulch.blog/2026/10/23/colorados-record-shattering-water-year-was-ridiculously-warm-a-little-bit-scary-and-offered-a-new-perspective-on-how-climate-change-will/">record-high summer temperatures</a>.</p>

<p>Fall 2026’s heavy rain and snow may help make up for last year and start to <a href="https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-looms-large-over-us-winter-outlook">alleviate a long-running drought</a> that has been causing water supply problems across the western U.S. for a quarter century.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="U.S. map showing wetter than normal weather forecast across lower half of the US" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773161/original/file-20261119-62-dt9mj6.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook for November 2026 through February 2027 shows a high chance of above-normal precipitation across the southern tier and coasts of the U.S.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/long_range/seasonal.php?lead=1">NOAA Climate Prediction Center</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In a positive sign, <a href="https://www.sltrib.com/news/2026/10/26/lake-powell-has-been-rising/">Lake Powell rose</a> with the recent rains. Overall, the <a href="https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027">Super El Niño conditions being forecast</a> for 2026-27 are expected to bring <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/long_range/seasonal.php?lead=3">more than average rain and snow</a> this winter across much of the southern and central United States, where it’s also likely to alleviate drought.</p>

<h2>What happens in Chile …</h2>

<p>Snow scientists like me <a href="https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202610.0215.v1">keep an eye on the South American winter</a> in El Niño years like this because it can give us a sense of what’s coming for North America.</p>

<p>Keep in mind that El Niño has been strengthening over the past few months – including through the South American winter that just ended.</p>

<p>South America saw a <a href="https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202610.0215">huge amount of snow</a>, particularly in the central Chilean Andes. In some <a href="https://skiportillo.com/en/home/">areas like Portillo</a>, the snow accumulation was the deepest since the current drought began in 2010, and the deepest in the past 70 years north of Santiago at the top of the Limarí River.</p>





<p>The snow was a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/pictures/record-breaking-el-nio-brings-unprecedented-snow-chile-2026-10-13/">boon for Chile’s ski resorts</a>. Valle Nevado got over 24 feet (7.3 meters) of snow and <a href="https://www.tetongravity.com/valle-nevado-extends-2026-ski-season-december/">extended its ski season</a>, originally scheduled to end in early October, into early December. Even the extremely dry Atacama Desert saw widespread snow followed by an <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/08/nx-s1-6023812/chile-desert-el-nino">explosion of spring flowers</a>.</p>

<p>Historically, snowy winters in Chile have meant snowy winters for California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies, too. The warm El Niño ocean allows the atmosphere to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.5511">pick up more moisture in this zone than usual</a>, and this <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/programs/climate-adaptation-science-centers/regional-super-el-nino-impacts-southwest-us">brings snowstorms to the U.S. Southwest</a>.</p>

<p>If that pattern holds this winter, the southern and central parts of the West should see well-above-average snowpack and active ski seasons, and those dangerously depleted reservoirs will have a chance to at least partially refill.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290792/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Preventable vision loss affects more than a billion people globally - and uneven access to care is the major culprit</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770313/original/file-20261105-64-eoegvk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5472%2C3648&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Basic eye care is inaccessible or unaffordable in many parts of the world.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/portrait-of-young-woman-during-eye-examination-test-glasses-news-photo/2161284769?phrase=person%20getting%20fitted%20for%20glasses&amp;adppopup=true">Godong/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Around the world, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(20)30425-3">more than 1 billion people are living with vision loss</a> in their daily lives. For many, this means they don’t have the glasses they need to see clearly. For others, conditions such as <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/cataracts/symptoms-causes/syc-20353790">cataracts</a>, <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/glaucoma/symptoms-causes/syc-20372839">glaucoma</a>, <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/15246-macular-degeneration">macular degeneration</a> or <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/diabetic-retinopathy/symptoms-causes/syc-20371611">diabetic eye disease</a> have caused vision loss.</p>

<p>The burden of this problem is not shared equally – 55% of those experiencing vision loss are women and girls, 73% are <a href="https://www.iapb.org/learn/resources/causes-of-vision-loss/">ages 50 and older</a>, and 90% live in <a href="https://datatopics.worldbank.org/world-development-indicators/the-world-by-income-and-region.html">low- and middle-income countries</a>.</p>

<p>Age is the most important <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/blindness-and-visual-impairment">risk factor for vision loss</a>. Since <a href="https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2026/demo/P95-26-1.html">global populations are rapidly aging</a>, the number of people experiencing vision loss is expected to increase to <a href="https://visionatlas.iapb.org/global-data/">more than 1.7 billion</a> by 2050.</p>

<p>So this public health threat is growing. Yet, it’s also almost entirely avoidable.</p>

<p>We are both <a href="https://experts.umich.edu/540-david-hutton">population health researchers</a>, and one of us is an <a href="https://experts.umich.edu/4214-josh-ehrlich">opthamologist</a>. We also lead the <a href="https://misharc.org/">Michigan Sensory Health and Aging Research Collaborative</a> at the University of Michigan, where we have spent years working to advance vision and eye health for underserved populations in the U.S. and globally. Recent developments give us hope that real progress is within reach.</p>

<h2>A smart investment</h2>

<p>Losing vision quite literally affects how people see the world, and it also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(20)30488-5">increases their risk of other health issues</a>, including falls, depression and even dementia. The risk of mortality is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(20)30549-0">more than twice as high</a> for adults living with vision loss.</p>

<p>The upside is that about 80% of vision loss can be reversed or prevented with timely detection and treatment. In fact, most cases can be fixed with eyeglasses or cataract surgery, <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/blindness-and-visual-impairment">two of the most cost-effective interventions</a> in all of healthcare.</p>

<p>A recent report showed that eye care is not only important for health and well-being, but it is also a smart investment: Every dollar that low- and middle-income countries invest in eye health <a href="https://www.hollows.org/research-and-guides/value-of-vision-investing-in-eye-health/">returns US$28 to their economies</a>. This makes eye health easily one of the best deals in global health and development.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/rFnqGf6p_Mk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">In many low- and middle-income countries, an eye examination and a pair of glasses can be life-changing.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A development problem with a financial upside</h2>

<p>Back in 1999, the World Health Organization launched an initiative called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/archopht.122.4.615">VISION 2020: The Right to Sight</a>. The aim was to draw attention and resources to vision and eye health problems, including those that would affect an aging global population.</p>

<p>More recently, in 2021, 193 United Nations member countries <a href="https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3933853?ln=en&amp;v=pdf">unanimously ratified</a> a resolution calling on governments and international financial institutions to improve access to eye care and to provide the resources to make this possible.</p>

<p>In addition, this resolution acknowledged the central role of vision and eye health in achieving the <a href="https://sdgs.un.org/goals">U.N. sustainable development goals</a>, a set of 17 ambitious aims, including universal access to food, clean water, education and work. Reframing vision and eye health as a development issue with a massive financial upside put the problem in front of people from a variety of sectors, such as education, labor and economics, and encouraged them to imagine how they could be a part of the solution.</p>

<p>In the five years since that resolution passed, the eye health sector has evolved some innovative strategies. For example, the new <a href="https://visioncatalystfund.org/">Vision Catalyst Fund</a> brings together large-scale donors, nongovernmental organizations and local medical providers to test new approaches to paying for eye care and getting it to those most in need.</p>

<p>Another organization that has emerged to tackle avoidable vision loss is <a href="https://peekvision.org/">Peek Vision</a>, a U.K.-based charity that began as a simple smartphone app. This app can be used by anyone with access to a smartphone to screen vision. So far, it has been used to <a href="https://peekvision.org/annual-reviews/">screen more than 18 million people</a> for vision loss and has connected more than 1.5 million to eye care. The organization is hoping to screen a million people per week by 2029.</p>

<h2>Building momentum</h2>

<p>In November 2026, the government of Antigua and Barbuda hosted the first-ever <a href="https://globalsummitforeyehealth.org/">Global Summit for Eye Health</a>, in collaboration with the governments of Nigeria, Guyana, Ireland and Bangladesh and the WHO. Policymakers, nongovernmental organizations, heads of state and global organizations such as the U.N., WHO and World Bank attended, with an eye toward a singular goal – ending avoidable sight loss worldwide.</p>

<p>The summit’s goal was to bring together key players from across the eye health sector. Governments and organizations are being asked to <a href="https://globalsummitforeyehealth.org/policy/view-the-commitments/">make forward-looking commitments</a> toward accelerating progress. For example, 48 governments committed to embedding eye health in their national health systems, while health ministries, NGOs and eye hospitals have committed to providing cataract surgery and eyeglasses to tens of millions of people over the next few years.</p>

<p>The evidence to drive this investment is already there: Trials have shown that vision care for kids <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2021.3544">boosts educational outcomes</a>. In middle-aged and older adults, research shows that an inexpensive pair of reading glasses boosts productivity and economic earnings in the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(18)30329-2">agricultural</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bjo-2025-328563">garment</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0296115">artisan</a> industries. </p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Affording eye care in the US</h2>

<p>While low- and middle-income countries contend with the overwhelming majority of vision loss, the problem is also significant in the U.S., where an estimated <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/vision-health-data/prevalence-estimates/vision-loss-prevalence.html">32.2 million people contend with vision loss</a>.</p>

<p>Older adults are by far the most affected group. While they benefit from Medicare coverage for medical issues such as cataracts, glaucoma and macular degeneration, major gaps remain, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.59071">unequal access to advanced eye care</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2018.2524">inconsistent coverage of eyeglasses</a> by Medicare.</p>

<p>Under traditional Medicare, <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/eyeglasses-contact-lenses">eyeglasses are covered only once</a> in a beneficiary’s lifetime, following cataract surgery. Otherwise, glasses can be a large – and recurring – out-of-pocket expense. With a pair of glasses <a href="https://visionatlas.iapb.org/country-data/united-states/">costing an average of US$200-$370</a> in the U.S., compared with <a href="https://visionatlas.iapb.org/country-data/china/">roughly $35 in China</a> <a href="https://visionatlas.iapb.org/country-data/india/">or India</a>, clear eyesight may be financially out of reach for many older Americans. Low-cost online retailers have helped to disrupt this market, but accessing glasses through those websites still requires internet access and a credit or debit card.</p>

<p>Older adults dealing with common issues such as cataracts or <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/24224-refractive-errors">refractive error</a>, which causes blurry vision, are at higher risk for all sorts of costly downstream health issues, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/jgs.18879">including falls</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01296-0">dementia</a>. Each year in the U.S., 2.3 million older adults wind up in the ER for a fall, and nearly 1 million are admitted to the hospital, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.injury.2023.111199">costing the healthcare system about $20 billion</a>. When it comes to dementia, <a href="https://schaeffer.usc.edu/research/the-cost-of-dementia-in-2025/">the costs are even greater</a>, at around $750 billion dollars per year.</p>

<p>Financing more comprehensive <a href="https://ihpi.umich.edu/news-events/news/policy-brief-value-vision-care-potential-health-and-economic-benefits-addressing">eye care for older Americans</a> is actually in everyone’s best interest. In fact, every dollar that public programs such as Medicare invest in treating refractive error and cataracts in older Americans is likely to return $9 to the U.S. economy. Annually, this equates to around $23 billion. This return on investment comes in the form of increased economic productivity, medical cost savings, fewer falls and fewer people with dementia.</p>

<p>Being able to see clearly is essential to overall health and well-being. The data is clear, that regardless of a country’s level of wealth, it makes sense to put resources toward vision and eye health.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294770/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Why everyone, even the GOP, is sick of JD Vance
excerpt: President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance at a Veterans Day in Arlington National Cemetery on November 11, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images This stor
body: President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance at a Veterans Day in Arlington National Cemetery on November 11, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Remember two weeks ago, when Vice President JD Vance was having a bad week ? It’s gotten much, much worse.  Vance has spent most of the last two years as the MAGA movement’s heir apparent — so much so that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, potentially his top rival for the 2028 GOP presidential nomination, told a reporter last year that “If JD Vance runs for president, he’s going to be our nominee, and I’ll be one of the first people to support him.” Suffice to say, that no longer looks like the case: Vance, more than any other potential Republican candidate in 2028, emerged from the midterms in bad political shape, and President Donald Trump has been putting him through hell ever since.  Specifically, Vance has found himself in a trap of his own making on two issues: The Iran war and immigration

In a long social media  post the day after the midterms, he blamed the war for his party’s electoral catastrophe; more recently, he described “bipartisan immigration reform” that would allow undocumented immigrants to stay in the country as “morally and electorally disastrous.” The problem with those two stances is that he’s still Trump’s vice president, and Trump refuses to admit that the Iran war was the wrong decision (though he’s been willing enough to concede that it was an electoral anchor)
Trump is also in the midst of showing occasional, vague interest in the aforementioned bipartisan immigration reform

And he’s reportedly not happy with Vance’s subtweets.   Both of those tensions were on full display Friday in a press conference by Trump, Vance, and Rubio, where Vance dodged a question on whether the war was worth the political fallout — an area where Trump has strongly suggested he’d like more backup from his second-in-command. “The president said he would do it again,” Vance told reporters. “My view is that my goal in my job is to support the president of the United States.”  That answer, you might correctly surmise, is almost certainly not going to do it with Trump over the long run. (This being the same president so bent on conforming the world around him to his views that he dispenses matching too-big shoes to his team, and they wear them.) Vance’s double bind Vance’s plight is particularly dire because he doesn’t really have anywhere to run

His options look something like this:  Hug Trump, hope for an endorsement, and see if the president’s reflected goodwill can push him to the nomination (and potentially to a general election wipeout, if Trump’s trajectory with voters stays the same);  Break from Trump more dramatically, forfeiting an endorsement and MAGA enthusiasm, and try to stake out his own brand in the primary and the general;  Or keep on keeping on, cryptically sniping at opponents from social media until Trump gets mad anyway
Meanwhile, the weaker Vance looks , the more his potential rivals are likely to eye the throne for themselves

In a poll released Thursday by Emerson College , Vance’s potential 2028 support has collapsed from 54 percent this time last year to just 20 percent, while Rubio’s has jumped from 6 percent to 36 percent (more than any other polled candidate, with Vance in second)
And Rubio, according to CNN , is leaving some people with the impression that he’s more open to a run
Other Republicans, including outgoing Florida Gov.  Ron DeSantis and Texas Sen

Ted Cruz, are also believed to be considering runs, and both would have the advantage of being able to run from outside a Trump administration that seems unlikely to grow more popular over the next two years.  Vance, in other words, already looks like he could be approaching his best-by date — and he still has a very long year-plus until the first votes are cast in the 2028 primary
