body: In Grand Theft Auto IV, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive There are plenty of reasons to be excited for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out today
There are the heists, the incredibly realistic depictions of Florida , the surprisingly deep romance , and, you know, the car theft
It’s been 13 years since the last installment of the incredibly popular game series — basically an eternity in 2026 terms
But personally, I’m interested in the pelicans in flight at sunset and the green scales of an iguana in the street, as seen in the game’s second trailer
There are more than 170 animals in the game, like alligators, manatees, and frogs
There are also 62 species of birds, and players can pull out binoculars and record them all in a logbook.  Now I’m not a video game writer
So this stuff is basically catnip for me, and I’m not the only one

There are Reddit threads full of excited birdwatchers who are saying that crime sprees will come second to birding in the new game, or that they want to get one of the game’s protagonists, Lucia, some cute birding outfits
The top comment in the New York Times’s review of the game says, “my roommate gets to play the actual game
I get to find all 67 [sic] species of birds

Truly a game for everyone.” features more than 170 species. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive" data-portal-copyright="Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive" /> While most of the game takes place in Vice City, which is developer Rockstar’s take on Miami, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades and other national parks
In real life, this is one of the richest ecosystems in the country; Florida is home to more than 700 terrestrial animals , thousands of fish, and over 500 species of migratory and year-round birds

And with GTA VI, Rockstar is going even more immersive than it did in another one of its games, Red Dead Redemption 2, by adding features like bioluminescence, feather types, and accurately depicting how hair and fur are rendered for its wide variety of animals.  View this post on Instagram “Florida has a diverse animal ecosystem that we wanted to faithfully include across all the different biomes in Leonida — urban and rural environs, aquatic life both inland and ocean, and the wetland habitats like the swamps and Everglades,” Rockstar’s vice president of dynamic art, Michael Kane, told Game Informer back in September (I reached out to Rockstar for comment but didn’t hear back by publication time)

I wouldn’t be surprised if some people spend way longer than strictly necessary wandering around in the opening areas, looking for one last bird to strike off their list.  Honestly, even though I’d call myself a gamer , I wasn’t entirely sure I’d play GTA VI
There’s just so much hype, and I was expecting it to mostly be another super-violent game about committing crimes
And of course that is part of it, but I love how it also seems to give people the option to take a moment and appreciate the natural world
To be fair, the game will also feature hunting of some of these animals, but I personally will be steering away from the Teddy Roosevelt school of conservation
It’s not the kind of thing you’d expect from a triple-A blockbuster, and maybe it’ll even get players to care more about biodiversity

Who knows, maybe afterward they’ll be motivated to, you know, touch grass.  “We’ve been painting birds on the walls of caves and writing songs about them for millennia, and it makes total sense to me that this sort of wonder that we get from birds would find an expression in the very contemporary form of art that is a video game,” said Ethan Linck , an assistant professor in the Department of Ecology at Montana State University who stressed that he is not a gamer himself. “I could totally see someone who might not have any background in natural history or birdwatching get into this fun diversion in the game and then discover that they can basically do the exact same thing in real life using apps like eBird and iNaturalist
It’s no longer an old-person hobby.” Speaking of which, I have to go explore the Everglades myself

title: Teachers are reeling from an existential crisis. You’re probably feeling it too.
excerpt: Her fifth year of elementary school teaching at a public school in Indiana was, by far, her hardest
body: Her fifth year of elementary school teaching at a public school in Indiana was, by far, her hardest

It was 2022, the first full academic year without Covid restrictions, and her fourth-graders’ social skills were “pretty much nonexistent,” she told Vox. “Because they had spent so much time at home doing whatever they want to do, [they] didn’t have structure and didn’t know when a teacher tells you no, that means no,” Wimbley, now 29, said

Wimbley could see their exhaustion and empathized with the intensity of spending so much time with their kid during the pandemic. “I had parents blaming me for their child’s reading level, their child’s inability to do basic math, and I mean everything,” she said

One parent blamed her for the fact that her fourth-grader read at a kindergarten level. “I was like, ‘That’s not my fault.’” Right before spring break, Wimbley wrestled with whether this career she had felt called to — growing up, she idolized Miss Honey from Matilda — was even right for her anymore
And then a few days later, she was punched by a student. “After that, I was like, ‘Okay, I’m done
Why I reported this A few years ago, one of my best friends left her job as a middle-school math teacher
For nearly a decade, she’d loved it — and, as her friend, I found her extremely suited to the job
After the pandemic, however, she decided to make a pivot into a new field altogether
Her reasons for leaving echo what many teachers told me: a lack of accountability among students and their parents
Education is having a tough time hanging onto talent
According to one recent survey, one in four K-12 teachers said they’re very or somewhat likely to leave their job within the next year

Nearly 70 percent of teachers with less than five years of experience have considered leaving or already left the field because of poor working conditions, a lack of support, and low pay, another survey found
The core functions of the job have changed dramatically, too
Smartphones, computers, and AI make it difficult to keep students’ attention
After years of remote or hybrid schooling during the pandemic, teachers said many students struggle with accountability and basic social skills

A focus on scores and teaching to the test have constrained educators’ ability to reach students.   But teachers aren’t the only ones facing an existential career crisis.  So many workers are feeling burned out and emotionally beat down

Americans uniquely derive a lot of meaning from their jobs — so much so that they are often defined by them . “People who have the most meaningful jobs — personally meaningful — and it’s a calling, you do it with a sense of self-sacrifice and you’re willing to do it for fewer benefits, lower pay, and you spend more hours [there] ,” said Sarah Wittman , a professor of management at the Costello College of Business at George Mason University. “That’s often the case with teachers.”  The problems that educators face are a microcosm of the system problems that similarly plague any person working for a living in America today.  According to Gallup, 51 percent of US employees were either actively looking for a new job or keeping an eye out for new opportunities last year, a rate that increases to 61 percent of Gen Z workers
Food service and hospitality were among the top industries workers fled over the last few months
In a 2024 survey, 40 percent of nurses said they’d leave the workforce by 2029

Amid the Great Resignation of 2021, a Pew Research Center survey found that people left their jobs because of low pay, no room for growth, and feelings of disrespect.   That teaching, nursing and medical care, and hospital workers are at their wit’s end highlights the truth of burnout: it’s often the careers that give the most back to society that are susceptible to it.  And if we can’t collectively agree to support these professionals, who will our society go to bat for? In America, what careers are sustainable? The fundamental role of teachers has changed Since the 1890s, the typical school day in America has been fairly standardized
Teachers had their own classrooms, taught clearly defined courses — like science, geography, and math — assigned homework, graded tests, and sent home report cards
Instructors were the authority in their classrooms: they lectured, told students what to do and when, and set the standard for achievement.  More than a century later, educators had lost that control
Some report struggling with increased workloads and burnout, and, notably, after the pandemic, have seen increased student disruptions in the classroom, according to one study
Nearly all teachers in one survey said students use technology in the classroom , effectively transforming the job from a tactile one to a digital one

Smartphones, computers, and AI make it difficult to keep students’ attention.  Teachers must not only contend with distracted kids , but also take on the added responsibility of making their lessons engaging enough despite the screens
They wage constant battles with students who exclusively rely on AI for course work and who watch thousands of non-educational YouTube videos throughout the school day
Sometimes instructors are told the screens are the lesson
During her final year of teaching, Wimbley had several students who didn’t understand English; they were fluent in French, Chinese, Spanish, and Haitian Creole — languages she did not speak
She did her best to communicate, using Google Translate to teach them; her goal for the year was for these students to at least know the American English alphabet, she said

When she reached out to the school’s English as a New Language (ENL) teacher for assistance, Wimbley was told to let the kids watch YouTube all day. “And to not worry about it,” she said. “I was like, ‘I can’t do that

That’s not happening.’” (In Indiana, where Wimbley worked, K-12 educators are required to teach language arts, mathematics, social studies, sciences, fine arts, and health and physical education, in addition to other topics.) While Wimbley’s experience is egregious, insufficient funding has left classrooms across the US without crucial support , like teachers’ aides and ENL instructors
Public schools in America are supported by local, state, and federal governments
On a local level, property taxes help fund schools, which means wealthier areas receive more money

Districts with high poverty and greater populations of Black and Latinx students receive less funding than wealthier, majority-white areas.  Each state differs in their approach to school funding, but state legislatures determine how much money schools will receive from taxes and state contributions
More spending per child is associated with higher test scores and a greater likelihood of a student attending college
States like New York and Vermont spend over $25,000 per student , compared to less than half that in North Carolina and Idaho
Federal dollars account for only a small fraction of overall funding
During the Great Recession in 2008, some states cut taxes and, subsequently, public school budgets ; more than 350,000 K-12 teacher positions were eliminated
Even as an infusion of federal funds during the Covid-19 pandemic expired, many states cut taxes between 2021 and 2023, further depressing school budgets

Now, as enrollment plummets in districts nationwide, schools continue to struggle to keep up with costs , resulting in staff layoffs and school closures despite the fact that during the 2024-25 school year, over a third of public schools reported having one or more teacher job vacancies

title: Barns full of birds from America’s biggest foie gras company just burned down
excerpt: As this photo from the Monticello Fire Department captured, a sprawling fire burned down several barns at Hudson Valley Foie Gras, America’s largest foie gras p
body: As this photo from the Monticello Fire Department captured, a sprawling fire burned down several barns at Hudson Valley Foie Gras, America’s largest foie gras producer. | Monticello Fire Department Early Thursday morning in upstate New York, a fire broke out at Hudson Valley Foie Gras — the largest US producer of foie gras

French for “fatty liver,” foie gras is a delicacy product that’s made by force-feeding ducks in the final weeks of their lives.  The fire destroyed multiple barns, and while hundreds of young ducks and geese survived, it’s still unknown how many died. Commercial duck farms tend to house thousands of animals — and sometimes over 10,000 animals — per barn. “The fire took off so fast, there was no way to get inside to stop the spread,” Charlie Kalinowski, chief of the Smallwood/Mongaup Valley Fire Department, told Radio Catskill
Approximately 200 first responders from 37 fire departments responded to the blaze, and no humans were injured

Hudson Valley Foie Gras didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, though a vice president at the company told Radio Catskill that they suspect it started due to an electrical malfunction, which hasn’t been confirmed by local fire officials

Allie Granger of the nonprofit Animal Welfare Institute told Vox that the cause of barn fires usually goes unreported, but when they are reported, electrical malfunction tends to be among the most common causes at relatively large operations like Hudson Valley Foie Gras
This incident is expected to hit the US foie gras supply hard, as Hudson Valley Foie Gras is one of just two major US producers
The fire came weeks after voters in Washington, DC, and Denver, Colorado, voted to ban the sale of foie gras
Foie gras sales have also been banned in California; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Portland, Oregon; New York City; and the country of Brazil
The fire may get a relatively large amount of press attention, given the decades-long controversy over foie gras and recent votes on the product
But barn fires are a surprisingly common occurrence in the US livestock sector, killing hundreds of thousands to over a million animals each year
Some steps could be taken to reduce that number, though the meat, milk, and egg industries have largely opposed reforms
America’s industrial barn fire problem, briefly explained  In 2026, according to the Animal Welfare Institute, more than 1.2 million animals have already died in over 80 farm fires in the US

About 1 million of them died when several barns burned down at a massive egg farm in Iowa in March.  All told, more than 10 million farmed animals have died in fires in the US since 2013, which AWI believes is an undercount since reporting requirements vary by state.  When fires break out at farms, there’s usually no escape route for the animals

As I wrote in 2024: Virtually all animals raised for meat, dairy, and eggs in the US are raised on factory farms, where thousands to tens of thousands of animals are crammed together in large warehouses
These aren’t the old red barns you might see from the highway, anachronisms from a pre-industrial age
These contain modern ventilation, lighting, and heating systems that can malfunction and start a fire
According to the National Fire Protection Association, malfunctioning heating and electrical systems are the leading cause of US barn fires
The organization writes fire codes and standards, which are then adopted by states and localities, and they have a code for animal housing facilities, which covers farms

Granger told me it includes guidelines for sprinkler systems, building construction and materials, smoke detection, fire alarm systems and notification, among other measures.  In 2024, the National Fire Protection Association voted to update its animal housing code to require sprinklers in large barns
Industry trade groups representing the egg, pork, and chicken meat industries opposed the decision
The vote was arguably symbolic, though; farmers would only need to follow it in states that have adopted the code

According to NFPA, only nine states have — New York isn’t one of them — and several of these actually exempt farms from it. (Among the states that don’t exempt farms, it’s unclear whether the sprinkler requirement is being enforced

The NFPA didn’t immediately respond to questions.) Industry groups have argued that sprinkler systems would be too costly , that some farms may not have the water infrastructure to supply them in the event of a fire, and that other fire prevention and mitigation measures are sufficient

It’s currently unknown whether or not Hudson Valley Foie Gras’s barns had sprinkler systems. “We require sprinklers in so many different facilities across the United States,” Granger said. “They have been proven to be lifesaving.” The ducks and geese that died in the fire at Hudson Valley Foie Gras this week were of course destined to be slaughtered
But their deaths are a reminder of how little we know about the lives and safety of the animals US farms raise for our meat, milk, and egg supply.

title: Gen Z is getting nostalgic for the Obama era — with an asterisk
excerpt: “Millennial optimism exists because Obama won elections so decisively that they had time to hit the club afterward,” Olivia Julianna, a Democratic strategist an
body: “Millennial optimism exists because Obama won elections so decisively that they had time to hit the club afterward,” Olivia Julianna, a Democratic strategist and content creator, said. | Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images Millennial optimism is making a comeback online, thanks to the Democrats’ blue tsunami in this month’s midterm election

Social media is filled with videos, songs, and edits celebrating the midterms and linking the feeling to Barack Obama’s victories and the various cultural signifiers of the time, from indie bands to “ girlboss” CEOs
Many of them are produced by Gen Z users who have little memory of the era themselves
To some left-leaning millennials, it’s a teachable moment
On Instagram the day after the election, 37-year-old Rep

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) gave her younger followers a lesson in the roots of “millennial cringe,” that mix of hope and earnestness that Gen Zers often see as cloying and naive. “Imagine all the seats we flipped last night, that feeling, plus on top of it, electing the first Black president ever
And on top of that, you did it the first time you ever voted? That hits generationally ,” Ocasio-Cortez said . “Like, you are chasing that feeling ever since
And because you did it the first time you ever voted, you’re like, ‘Yeah, we can change the world

Why not just do it again?’” But while some millennials (including many of the victorious candidates ) might proudly claim this moment as a restoration of their culture — everyone back to Hamilton ! — some of the Gen Z voters and operatives who helped power their wins are also trying to carve out their own lane

Rather than a straightforward revival, these Gen Z are calling their experience “ WhimZ ,” which they see as distinct from millennial optimism, and hardened by their own divergent experiences in the Trump era
Unlike millennial optimism — rooted in the fact that if you believe in change and progress and work to make it possible, it will come — Gen Z liberals know that’s not the case

And indeed, there’s a sharp satirical edge to some of the stomp-clap celebrations making the rounds.  Obama’s young voters struggled to keep up the same energy, urgency, and turnout (the 2014 midterms had historically low participation) when he wasn’t on the ballot, in part — in “WhimZ’s” telling — because they were overly confident that emerging trends in technology, social media, and culture might solve problems and eliminate discrimination for them. “Gen Z’s ‘WhimZ’ is very different than millennial optimism and the reason why is us as Gen Z know that we still have to fight,” TikToker @bearclawharley explained in one video. “This is no hate to millennials; you guys were promised…follow the rules and you guys will get a good job and yada yada
We as Gen Z know that that’s not going to happen
You guys were just carefree; we are ironically doing this.” First-time voters in 2026 were born the year Obama was elected and just 8 years old when Trump was elected in 2016

They’ve grown up in a divisive political climate and understand that even when you march, protest, organize, and ultimately vote — you don’t always get the outcome you want.  Lauren Kapp, who co-founded the Democratic digital strategy firm Luminary Strategies and helped with the James Talarico campaign’s social media operation this midterms, said one of her own core political memories was walking into her high school class after the 2016 election and seeing her AP government teacher in tears. “Political instability has left Gen Z burned,” Kapp said. “We’ve had to cope through our humor as a matter of processing
To me, WhimZ is less about believing things will get better and more about finding moments of joy despite the uncertainty.” “Political instability has left Gen Z burned

We’ve had to cope through our humor as a matter of processing.” Lauren Kapp, co-founder of the Democratic digital strategy firm Luminary Strategies The rising generation is also not as liberal or partisan — in fact, more than half (56 percent) of Zoomers identify as independent , according to Gallup — and those who do tilt left are more comfortable with anti-establishment voices, like the rising socialist movement , than their elders are
They care far less about party labels and far more about results

According to Olivia Julianna, a Democratic strategist and content creator, millennial optimism is “more institutional than WhimZ.” “Millennial optimism exists because Obama won elections so decisively that they had time to hit the club afterward

Then they could go to urgent care for IV fluids on their parents’ health insurance the next morning,” she said, alluding to Gen Z’s lack of trust across institutions. “WhimZ comes from a place that’s a little more vengeful

Our greatest victories have largely come from stopping the worst shit from happening instead of witnessing massive moments of inspiration from people in power or elected officials.” Rather than remembering elections as their touchstones, Gen Z’s core political memories have been direct actions they took themselves: March for Our Lives, Black Lives Matter, climate protests, or more recently, organized action against ICE

This sentiment comes up repeatedly in conversations and focus groups with younger voters as part of my research work: Voting the right politicians into office is not enough. “We know that we have a lot to work on and flipping this is a good first step but definitely just a first step,” one 22-year-old woman from Denver told me after the midterms.  “Most of the gains Gen Z has seen in the political atmosphere we’ve grown up amid [and] have come to know have been temporary and marginal,” a 21-year-old woman from New York City told me. “I think we have more cautious optimism about the trajectory of the [country], rather than millennials’ sheer optimism.” Where the two generations come together perhaps is a shared recognition that anger, nihilism, and retreat are not the answer

In focus groups last spring, I started hearing fed-up young Americans tell me they were looking for candidates who offered a forward-looking vision on issues they care about — the economy, war, corruption, AI — rather than those who lament the opposite party or rationalize the status quo

And as the midterm cycle went on, it became clearer that they were over the culture war , and instead, interested in candidates who unite in service of fighting these core issues, rather than those who try to divide voters along identity or partisan lines.  It sounds cheesy for a generation that’s known for being so wildly jaded
And having grown up in a political ecosystem dominated by bullying, for Gen Z, a “ politics of love ” (as Talarico describes it) feels brand new
They may not be ready to let their guard down like their millennial forebears, but there’s a realization that hate, fear, and division haven’t gotten us very far.

title: How Uruguay built a national care system from the ground up
excerpt: Imagine a family with two working parents who can drop off their 2-year-old at a neighborhood childcare center for the workday for little to no fee
body: Imagine a family with two working parents who can drop off their 2-year-old at a neighborhood childcare center for the workday for little to no fee
Their 4-year-old goes to a free public preschool nearby
Across town, the mother’s 82-year-old father, who can no longer bathe or dress himself, is visited by a personal assistant the government mostly pays for, 80 hours a month
It’s not a daydream, it’s just a normal day for many families in Uruguay.  And it is not just for lower-income households

A little more than a decade ago, Uruguay passed a law declaring that care for children, seniors, people with disabilities, and caregivers themselves is a right, and has been working to make good on that promise ever since

The resulting National Integrated Care System, known as SNIC (Sistema Nacional Integrado de Cuidados), has become a model around the world for treating care not as a privilege but as public infrastructure

Across the country of about 3.4 million people, the system now provides early childhood care for some 78,000 children , subsidized home assistants for more than 6,000 people with severe disabilities, and day centers and emergency call services for older adults — through a network of community-run childcare centers, certified care workers, and a national agency that coordinates it all
The undertaking has been huge, and the buildout is still in process

But the reasons for it echo across other high-income countries right now, including the United States, namely: falling birth rates, an aging population, and generations of women who are no longer willing or able to provide care for free.  Key takeaways Uruguay was the first Latin American country to make care a legal right, with one national system covering children, older adults, people with disabilities, and caregivers themselves
It took decades of feminist organizing, so the plan was ready when a sympathetic government took power
Writing it into law helped it survive a change in government, but Uruguay is still working out how to pay for broader access
The US faces the same demographic squeeze and has started building some of the same pieces, from Washington’s long-term care insurance to universal childcare in New Mexico

Uruguay sees this sprawling care system as a matter of rights but also as an economic investment, creating paid care jobs and enabling more women to enter formal employment, where they can then pay into the pension and health systems that an otherwise shrinking workforce needs to support. (The law itself lists among its goals changing “the current sexual division of labor” — the fact that care work falls overwhelmingly on women and is usually unpaid.) Leaders now describe SNIC as the “fourth pillar” of its social protection system, alongside education, social security, and healthcare.  “It’s the closest thing I could find globally to an idea that family care — not unlike Social Security and Medicare — could be addressed through social insurance,” Ai-jen Poo, co-founder of US-based advocacy group Caring Across Generations, told me

Although Uruguay describes this care system as a right rather than an insurance program, she said, “the material manifestation is very similar.” Poo isn’t the only care activist in the US looking to Uruguay’s example

Holly Milburn-Smith, the co-executive director of the City Hub and Network for Gender Equity (CHANGE), which works with cities on care policy, told me Uruguay’s appeal is partly that its example can’t be waved away the way policies in Nordic countries often are for relying on high taxation rates Americans would be hard pressed to accept. “We’re not talking about Scandinavian countries, we’re talking about Latin American countries,” she said
And in Uruguay, “they have found a way to do something that we haven’t.” Uruguay’s system is neither perfect nor finished
It still mostly serves children, the waitlist for home assistants is long, and its leaders are still fighting over how to fully pay for it
But the country has built something with lessons for all of us, revealing both the promise and the challenges of treating caregiving as a public good
How did Uruguay get this done? Uruguay’s ambitious public care system was decades in the making
The country has had both the needs and many of the means to make it happen
It has one of the oldest populations in the region, and its fertility rate is estimated at just 1.2 children per woman , well below the roughly two needed for each generation to replace itself
So Uruguay has more older people who need help, fewer workers to pay for it, and smaller families to fall back on — the same squeeze the US is heading into

The country is also among the most wealthy and most economically equal nations in Latin America, and has had a proud welfare state tradition dating back to the early 1900s, with left-leaning governments for most of the last two decades.  But Argentina, Brazil, and Chile all also had left-wing governments in the late 2000s and early 2010s, and none of them built a national care system then

What set Uruguay apart was “decades of political organizing” by feminist organizations, researchers, care advocates, and public officials who built a shared agenda, Michael Touchton, a political scientist who has spent two decades studying Latin American governance, told me.  The feminist organizing was fueled by data

Sociologists at the Universidad de la República , the country’s public university, ran the country’s first time-use survey in 2003, which aimed to identify the kinds of unpaid care work and household labor that so often goes unmeasured and unnoticed in economic analyses

Led by researchers Rosario Aguirre and Karina Batthyány, the survey found that women in Montevideo and its metropolitan area were doing about two-thirds of all unpaid work , and that once paid and unpaid work were added together, women were working six hours a week more than men.  (The US launched its own first national time-use survey the same year and found a similar pattern: For example, in homes with a child under 6, women worked on average 2.7 hours a day on childcare to men’s 1.2.)  Following that early research, feminist organizations, other academics, union members, and female legislators in Uruguay spent the late 2000s pushing care onto the national agenda, holding public forums, and working through a cross-party caucus of female legislators ahead of the 2009 election
Their pressure was successful, with all four parties that had seats in parliament ultimately mentioning care in their platforms
But it was women inside the Frente Amplio , the left-wing coalition that had governed Uruguay since 2005, who got their party to commit to something more concrete
Frente Amplio’s 2009 platform promised “a truly comprehensive system of family care,” and when the party won again that year, it finally had a mandate to build one

After a national debate over what “care” even meant — teachers didn’t want to be lumped in with care workers, and feminists fought to keep gender at the center of the legislation — the law passed in 2015, with support across party lines.  These coalitional fights helped shape what the law itself ultimately said, with three decisions standing out
First, the SNIC would provide services rather than cash to families, out of concern that paying families would simply subsidize the status quo, with women still doing the lion’s share of the work
Second, the SNIC would treat care as a right for everyone rather than a benefit for the poorest — a break from the means-based approach Latin American welfare states have usually embraced
And third, Uruguay’s care infrastructure would be written into law rather than left to regulation, which is harder to overturn

The next was turning the law into something real — and that would last.   Inside Uruguay’s care system The Scandinavian countries are often held up as the pinnacle of public caregiving, with childcare and eldercare guaranteed as entitlements and funded by some of the highest taxes in the world
Uruguay, however, does not have such markedly high tax rates as northern Europe

It has instead positioned care as what the law calls a “co-responsibility,” in which the state regulates and helps fund care but shares the jobs with families, communities, employers, and private providers.  To do this, the government pulled existing services into a single system

In practice, this looks like neighborhood childcare centers run by community organizations under contract with the state, home assistants hired by families and subsidized on a sliding scale by income, and, for example, a childcare center for construction workers’ children funded by the industry’s employers under an agreement with their union.  Uruguay’s care infrastructure remains a work in progress

The country spends less than 0.1 percent of its GDP on long-term care (ongoing help with daily life for older adults and people with disabilities), but a government-convened commission estimated that universal coverage would require roughly 10 times that
More than 7,000 people are currently on a waitlist for subsidized personal care assistants

Part of the challenge is the National Integrated Care System has no dedicated revenue stream, unlike pensions (funded by mandatory wage contributions), healthcare (which runs through social security), or education (which has its own budget)

title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
excerpt: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replan
body: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover
The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
excerpt: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power
body: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament
In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday

title: The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks
They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste
The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones
Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive . —Antonio Regalado What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion
The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market
But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted
The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition
Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter

title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
excerpt: Record-breaking liver survival: A Sydney surgical team kept a human liver alive outside the body for seven weeks using an automated system of pumps and sensors
body: Record-breaking liver survival: A Sydney surgical team kept a human liver alive outside the body for seven weeks using an automated system of pumps and sensors that mimics the functions of a living body

Automation was the secret: When the team compared manual versus automated life-support systems across 55 donated livers, automated perfusion tripled average survival time to four weeks, with one organ reaching seven
Organs that heal: Organ perfusion has become more common over the past decade
Researchers have found some evidence that extended perfusion may allow damaged organs to repair themselves before transplant
A new frontier in medicine: Long-term organ life-support is attracting serious scientific interest

Two new scientific societies were recently founded to explore the concept. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148934" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.  In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.    Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C
The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago
That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.  Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination
Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ
This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.  Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving
During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other

Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.   Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body

Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.   While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.” Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual
One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so

That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days
What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months

He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.   Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon

Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods
For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs
In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else
After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume
Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine

If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs. “It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”   He’s not the only one who thinks so
For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps
The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them
That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says
Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs , a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body

Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body
Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept
One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy

The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “ organ medicine” : research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”   “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
excerpt: A billion-dollar battery deal: Sila, a US battery materials startup, has signed a major supply agreement with Panasonic Energy worth potentially over $1 billion
body: A billion-dollar battery deal: Sila, a US battery materials startup, has signed a major supply agreement with Panasonic Energy worth potentially over $1 billion, marking its first mass-market deal

Better batteries, lighter and faster: Sila's silicon-carbon anode material weighs a fifth as much as conventional graphite and cuts volume in half, enabling batteries that pack more energy, charge faster, and could extend EV range significantly

Geopolitics, not climate, is driving the money: With China controlling over 90% of graphite production, the Trump administration's Defense Department backed Sila with a $1.4 billion loan—framing batteries as a national security issue rather than a climate solution. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148922" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US
Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries
It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time
This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately
A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department
While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics
Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries
The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company
So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example
The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years
My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021
Things have gotten a lot bigger since then

In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain
The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating
But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.   This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years
Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year
The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics
While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics
China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today
For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals

But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it
Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition

Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.) I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority. “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company
And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
excerpt: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at
body: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group

title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
excerpt: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating
body: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024

The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza

title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
excerpt: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere
body: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere
Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue
Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms

Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .  You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey
You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad

In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.
